title: Compute the Nth Fibonacci number, where each number is the sum of the two preceding ones. Explain the Fibonacci Numbers dynamic programming pattern, bottom-up versus memoization, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Fibonacci Numbers (Compute the Nth Fibonacci with Dynamic Programming)
keyPoints: The Fibonacci Numbers DP pattern covers problems where each state depends on a fixed window of previous states
Naive recursion is O(2^n) due to repeated subproblems; memoization makes it O(n) time and O(n) space
Bottom-up with two rolling variables gives O(n) time and O(1) space
Fibonacci numbers overflow long at n = 93, so production code uses BigInteger
The pattern generalises to climbing stairs, house robber, and any fixed-window recurrence
Matrix exponentiation computes fib(n) in O(log n) time for extremely large n

s1_definition.oneliner: Each state depends on the previous two; keep two rolling values for linear time and constant space.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Fibonacci Numbers pattern** – a DP family where each state depends on a fixed number of previous states.
- **Definition** – `fib(0) = 0`, `fib(1) = 1`, `fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)` for n >= 2.
- **Naive recursion** – O(2^n) time due to exponential recomputation of identical subproblems.
- **Memoization** – O(n) time and O(n) space by caching each result.
- **Bottom-up rolling** – O(n) time and O(1) space by keeping only the last two values.
- **Overflow** – Fibonacci numbers exceed long at n = 93; use BigInteger for exact results.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India models a simple compounding sequence where each month's projected figure is the sum of the two previous months. Instead of recomputing the whole history from scratch for every query, the system remembers just the last two months and rolls forward, computing the answer in one pass.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Fibonacci Numbers dynamic programming pattern covers problems where each state depends on a fixed window of previous states. The classic Fibonacci sequence is the simplest example, but the pattern extends to climbing stairs, house robber, decode ways, and any fixed-window recurrence.

Naive recursion creates an exponential call tree because it recomputes the same subproblems. Memoization fixes this by caching each result, reducing the work to O(n) time with O(n) space. The bottom-up rolling approach goes further: since each value depends only on the previous two, keep just two variables and iterate forward for O(n) time and O(1) space.

At the National Bank of India, the analytics team used this pattern for a reward-points projection where each month's target equalled the sum of the previous two months. The rolling computation returned results instantly even for distant future months, and popular results were cached in Redis for repeated queries.

The senior-level addition is that Fibonacci numbers overflow a long at n = 93, so BigInteger is necessary for large indices. Matrix exponentiation computes fib(n) in O(log n) time for extreme cases, but the rolling approach is what you use in practice.

Remember one sentence: each state depends on the previous two, so keep two rolling values for linear time and constant space.
